articles.title: SC restored people's faith: Kapil Sibal a day after venting frustration
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Supreme Court's order Sunday finding prima facie breach of its Oct 9 order against complete shutdown of Metro and train services and issuing
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Supreme Court's order Sunday finding prima facie breach of its Oct 9 order against complete shutdown of Metro and train services and issuing notice to Union home secretary, Delhi Police commissioner and Delhi Metro chief altered over the course of a day senior advocate and Rajya Sabha MP Kapil Sibal's views on the apex court.On Saturday, Sibal had told reporters "if we go to courts, I do not know whether we will ever get relief. The people of this country have decided that this govt has to go. If anyone can save the Constitution at this juncture, it is Supreme Court."He added, "I am tired of repeatedly approaching the SC. It's in my mind that there is no purpose in going there. I have not much expectations from SC. Whatever is to happen will happen. I only pray the country's democracy remains intact... The tribunals (in West Bengal) have allowed appeals of 93% voters whose names were deleted illegally. SC has come to know this. But we did not get any relief".On Sunday, he was leading a 100-strong team of lawyers in SC to question the detentions of protesters and alleged violations of court's Oct 9 order against shutdown of Metro and rail services. The emotionally charged arguments saw pro-protester lawyers paint a picture of injustice and violation of fundamental rights on Saturday, compare it to an "undeclared emergency" and shout down a senior advocate who said lawyers must confine their activities to courts and not hit the streets, and that freedom of speech came with reasonable restrictions.At an appropriate juncture, Justice Joymalya Bagchi said, "Our purpose is to instil people's faith in the system, and in that process your (lawyer's) confidence is most vital for our fight against injustice." The court also passed a slew of directives, including normalising Metro, train and internet services and traffic in the city and allowing lawyers and journalists to carry out professional work.Soon after the SC order, Sibal said, "We are deeply grateful to the Supreme Court for passing an order that restores the faith of the Indian people, as well as the faith of professionals, in the justice system of this country."Within an hour of SC passing the order, a senior advocate entered into an argument with cops over removal of barricades, citing the SC ruling. The order was yet to be made public and police personnel didn't know about it.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: ‘Punched in the eyes, pushed into bus’: Journalists detained for second day at CJP protest despite IDs
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: On a day SC said lawyers, journalists and other professionals should not be impeded from carrying out their professional duties, several
articles.body: NEW DELHI: On a day SC said lawyers, journalists and other professionals should not be impeded from carrying out their professional duties, several journalists covering the protests were detained for a second day running Sunday.Among those detained were those working for established media organisations as well as independent online portals.A photojournalist, who wo­rks for a news agency, told TOI: “I was covering the AISA protest at RK Ashram when police started dispersing everyone in the area. When only mediapersons remained, they started to drag us by our necks into police vans even after we displayed our IDs, our cameras and shouted that we were from the press.The van had 7-8 journalists when they shut the doors and started moving. After a few kilometres, the van had to stop as police were removing barricades to make way. That was when I and two other journalists jumped out.”Nitin Katiyar, a digital journalist with Nayab World, was detained from the Connaught Place roundabout while covering the students’ march. Showing cuts below his right eye, Katiyar said that police detained him despite his showing “valid media credentials”. He alleged he was pushed inside the bus, where police allegedly punched him in the eyes when he protested.Among those detained were three Indian Express Hindi journalists. The organisation said in a post on X: “Three journalists from Indian Express Hindi — Shashwat, Siya, and Vijay — have been detained by Delhi Police while reporting. Even after informing the police that they were journalists who had come to do their job, they were forcibly put into a bus. The police bus was passing through Connaught Place in Delhi when Shashwat sent us a video he recorded on his mobile camera. Our colleague Siya’s phone has been seized by the police.”The three were later let go at Chhatrasal Stadium, the media organisation said.Pragya Mishra, an Uttar Pradesh-based journalist with Bharat Samachar, was also detained while she was covering the protests Saturday. On X, she posted a video of 5-6 policewomen grabbing her arms and legs while detaining her.“Take people into custody. Make them sit in police stations. Stop those who are showing the truth. Don’t let the pictures of the rape of democracy go out. Delhi Police is working on this agenda. I have a mic, the mic ID is there. I have everything, but in an extremely humiliating manner, Delhi Police deliberately threw me inside the bus and detained me. This is the capital of the country...” she posted on X. A journalist working with The Hindu was also detained in the evening. Several YouTubers and content creators were detained throughout the day from different protest spots, including RK Ashram, Connaught Place and near Jantar Mantar.There was no response from police over the issue till the time of going to press.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Delhi | Silver Rate in Delhi | Bank Holidays in Delhi | Public Holidays in Delhi | Delhi AQI | Weather in Delhi | Petrol Price in Delhi | Diesel Price in Delhi | CNG Price in Delhi | LPG Price in DelhiStay updated with the latest Delhi news. articles.title: 12 Australian farming families were fined $814 each for blocking surveyors; they say a proposed 480-kilometre power line threatens their land
articles.summary: Twelve farming families in western Victoria, Australia, have been fined A$814 each for refusing to allow authorised officers onto their properties to
articles.body: Twelve farming families in western Victoria, Australia, have been fined A$814 each for refusing to allow authorised officers onto their properties to conduct surveys for a proposed 480-kilometre electricity transmission line. The families say the project, known as Victoria to New South Wales Interconnector West (VNI West), threatens agricultural land, farm operations and the future of properties that some have worked for generations. Another six landowners received formal warnings after denying access. The fines, issued in August 2026, have intensified opposition to the multibillion-dollar infrastructure project, with affected farmers challenging the government's approach to private property access. The dispute has since moved towards a legal challenge, while the project's environmental assessment remains underway.Why were 12 Australian farming families fined?The Victorian government issued the infringement notices on August 4, 2026, after the landholders refused access to authorised officers seeking to undertake preliminary investigations for VNI West. The notices alleged that the farmers had hindered, obstructed or delayed authorised activities without a reasonable excuse. The fines were issued under Victoria's Electricity Industry Act 2000, which provides powers for authorised officers to access land for specified electricity infrastructure planning activities. Six other property owners received formal warnings for refusing access.The farmers argue that their refusal was linked to concerns about the timing of inspections, agricultural activities and the potential consequences of the proposed transmission line. They maintain that they should have greater control over access to their properties, particularly when visits could interfere with livestock management or other time-sensitive farming work.What is the proposed 480-kilometre power line?VNI West is a proposed high-voltage transmission project designed to strengthen electricity connections between Victoria and New South Wales. It would connect renewable energy zones and electricity networks across the two states, helping transport power between generation sources and major demand centres. The Victorian section involves a proposed 500-kilovolt, double-circuit overhead transmission line running from the Bulgana area in western Victoria towards a terminal station at Tragowel, before continuing north towards the Murray River near Kerang. From there, the project would connect with infrastructure in New South Wales.The project is intended to improve electricity reliability, support the integration of renewable energy and provide access to generation and storage resources across state borders. Its estimated cost has been reported in the range of A7.6billiontoA11.4 billion for the wider project. However, the proposed route crosses agricultural regions where farming is a major economic activity. Landholders along the alignment have raised concerns about the placement of transmission towers, access tracks and easements, as well as the potential effects on land use and property values.Farmers fear damage to their land and livelihoodsFor the affected families, the dispute is not simply about surveyors entering their properties. They are concerned about what the eventual infrastructure could mean for their farms, businesses and the land they hope to pass on to future generations. Trent Carter, a fifth-generation sheep farmer from Wallaloo East in western Victoria, objected to surveyors entering a paddock during lambing season. He said the visit could put his stud Merino sheep at risk and argued that the authorities had not adequately considered animal welfare and the timing of agricultural operations.Carter said his family had attempted to negotiate a more suitable inspection time but felt their concerns were not properly addressed. He subsequently said he intended to contest the fine rather than pay it. Other landholders have raised concerns about the effect of transmission infrastructure on farm layouts, bushfire preparedness and the marketability of their properties. They fear that the presence of large towers and associated infrastructure could complicate agricultural operations and reduce the appeal of their land to prospective buyers.A 103-year-old farm and concerns about protected wildlifeColin and Mary Fenton, an elderly farming couple from the Kerang area, were among the landholders reported to have received fines. Their family has farmed the property for more than a century. Colin Fenton said the couple had raised concerns about a protected wedge-tailed eagle nest on their property. He questioned whether their objections had been adequately considered before the access notices were enforced.The couple also expressed concerns about the effect of the proposed project on their farm's value. Fenton said he had approached a real estate agent about selling the property but feared that the planned transmission infrastructure could make it harder to find a buyer. Their concerns highlight the broader questions surrounding the project's environmental assessment, including how wildlife habitats, agricultural land and existing land uses will be considered when the final route and associated infrastructure are determined.Farmers refuse to pay and prepare a legal challengeThe fines have prompted affected landholders to coordinate their response. Regional reporting in August indicated that the farmers intended to obtain legal representation and challenge the notices. By October 6, the Herald Sun reported that all 12 families had refused to pay and had secured an extension until October 23 after seeking an appeal through joint legal representation.The dispute centres partly on whether the farmers had a reasonable excuse for denying access and whether the enforcement measures were appropriate in the circumstances. The authorities maintain that authorised officers have legal powers to conduct specified planning activities and that landholders were notified of proposed visits. The legal challenge could bring greater scrutiny to how these powers are exercised when survey work affects active farms, including the consideration given to seasonal work, livestock welfare and biosecurity.The fines do not themselves determine whether the transmission project will ultimately be approved. They concern access for planning and survey activities, while the project's environmental and planning approvals follow a separate process.Government says survey access is necessary for planningVicGrid, the Victorian government body responsible for planning the state's transmission network, has argued that surveys are needed to understand the land and environmental conditions along the proposed route. Such investigations can examine biodiversity, waterways, cultural heritage, agriculture and other factors that may influence the project's design and potential impacts. The information is intended to inform the environmental assessment and identify measures to avoid or reduce harm.Authorities have said they sought voluntary access agreements with landholders before using statutory powers. The government has also pointed to notice periods and other engagement measures as part of its approach. The farmers, however, argue that notification alone does not adequately address their concerns when proposed visits conflict with critical farming activities. The disagreement has therefore become a test of how infrastructure planners balance statutory access rights with the practical realities of running agricultural businesses.Environmental assessment remains underwayThe Victorian component of VNI West is undergoing an environmental effects statement (EES), a detailed assessment of the project's potential environmental, social and economic consequences. The Victorian planning department says the EES was required in April 2024. It is intended to examine issues including biodiversity, native vegetation, cultural heritage, waterways, agriculture, land use and effects on communities.The EES went on public exhibition on October 5, 2026, with submissions open until November 16. An Inquiry and Advisory Committee directions hearing is scheduled for December 7, followed by a main hearing expected to begin in the week of February 8, 2027. The process will allow the project's evidence and public submissions to be considered before the planning minister makes the relevant assessment. The route and project design remain subject to the applicable assessment and approval requirements.For the farmers opposing the scheme, the assessment is a critical opportunity to have concerns about their land and livelihoods examined. For the project proponents, the process is intended to establish the likely effects of the infrastructure and determine how those effects can be managed.VNI West becomes a political issue in VictoriaOpposition to the transmission line has also become a point of political contention ahead of Victoria's November 2026 state election. In August, the Liberal and National parties pledged to scrap VNI West if the Coalition won the election, arguing that the project was not viable and that alternatives should be explored. The Victorian government defended the project, saying new transmission infrastructure would be important for electricity reliability as ageing coal-fired power stations retire. The debate reflects competing views about the future of Victoria's energy system. Supporters of VNI West say stronger interconnections are needed to transport renewable electricity and maintain reliable supply. Opponents question the project's cost, its effects on rural communities and whether alternative energy investments could achieve similar objectives.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Weather tomorrow: IMD predicts rain, thunderstorms and gusty winds in several states; Delhi, UP under alert
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The India Meteorological Department (IMD) has forecast rainfall, thunderstorms, lightning and gusty winds across several parts of India on
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The India Meteorological Department (IMD) has forecast rainfall, thunderstorms, lightning and gusty winds across several parts of India on Tuesday, October 13, with Delhi-NCR, Haryana, Punjab, Uttar Pradesh, Chhattisgarh and parts of south India likely to experience unsettled weather.Isolated to scattered rainfall is expected across several regions, while thunderstorms accompanied by gusty winds are likely in parts of northwest, central, eastern and southern India. Coastal Andhra Pradesh, Yanam and Rayalaseema may also experience strong surface winds during the ongoing weather spell.Rainfall activity is expected to continue across several states over the coming days, with parts of the Northeast, east India and south India likely to receive showers through October 18.IMD alert for TuesdayThe IMD has forecast isolated to scattered rainfall across several parts of northwest India, including Jammu and Kashmir, Ladakh, Himachal Pradesh, Uttarakhand, Punjab, Haryana, Chandigarh, Delhi and Uttar Pradesh.Chhattisgarh is also likely to receive isolated to scattered rainfall, accompanied by thunderstorms, lightning and gusty winds at isolated places on Tuesday.In east India, rainfall is likely over Jharkhand, Bihar and Odisha, while parts of the Andaman and Nicobar Islands may continue to receive showers. Several parts of south India are also likely to experience rainfall, thunderstorms and gusty winds.The IMD has forecast thunderstorms, lightning and gusty winds reaching 40-50 kmph, with gusts up to 60 kmph, over Chhattisgarh. Similar conditions are likely over Tamil Nadu, Puducherry and Karaikal during the October 12-15 period.Delhi-NCR weather tomorrowDelhi and the surrounding areas are likely to experience isolated to scattered rainfall on Tuesday, October 13, as part of the ongoing spell across northwest India.The IMD has forecast thunderstorms, lightning and gusty winds over Haryana, Chandigarh and Delhi during October 12-15. Gusty winds reaching 40-50 kmph, with gusts up to 60 kmph, are also likely during this period.The unsettled weather conditions may continue over the next few days, with rainfall expected across parts of the region through October 15.Uttar Pradesh weather tomorrowWest Uttar Pradesh is likely to receive isolated to scattered rainfall on Tuesday, with the wet spell expected to continue through October 16. The IMD has also forecast thunderstorms, lightning and gusty winds reaching 50-60 kmph at isolated places over West Uttar Pradesh during October 12-15.East Uttar Pradesh is likely to see rainfall activity on October 15 and 16.The forecast indicates that rainfall activity will continue across parts of Uttar Pradesh over the coming days, although the intensity and distribution may vary across the state.Punjab, Haryana and Rajasthan weatherPunjab is likely to receive isolated to scattered rainfall on Tuesday, with showers expected to continue through October 14. The IMD has also forecast thunderstorms, lightning and gusty winds over Punjab during October 12-15.Rainfall activity is likely to increase on October 15, when fairly widespread to widespread showers are forecast over Punjab.Haryana and Chandigarh are likely to experience rainfall and thunderstorms accompanied by gusty winds during October 12-15.West Rajasthan may receive isolated to scattered rainfall during the same period, with gusty winds reaching 30-40 kmph and gusts up to 50 kmph likely between October 13 and 15. East Rajasthan may receive isolated to scattered rainfall on October 13.Jammu and Kashmir, Himachal Pradesh and Uttarakhand weatherJammu and Kashmir, Ladakh and adjoining regions are likely to receive isolated to scattered rainfall on Tuesday. The IMD has forecast fairly widespread to widespread rainfall over Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh on October 13 and again on October 15.Himachal Pradesh is likely to experience isolated to scattered rainfall during October 12-13, followed by fairly widespread to widespread rainfall on October 14-15. Rainfall activity is also forecast to continue during October 16-18.Uttarakhand is likely to receive isolated to scattered rainfall during October 12-18.Thunderstorms and lightning are also likely over Jammu and Kashmir, Ladakh and adjoining regions during October 13-16, while Himachal Pradesh may experience similar conditions during October 12-15.Chhattisgarh weather forecastChhattisgarh is likely to receive isolated to scattered rainfall on Tuesday, with the wet spell expected to continue through October 18.The IMD has forecast thunderstorms, lightning and gusty winds reaching 40-50 kmph, with gusts up to 60 kmph, at isolated places over the state during October 12-13.Residents should remain alert to changing weather conditions during the ongoing spell.Jharkhand, Bihar and Odisha weatherJharkhand is likely to receive isolated to scattered rainfall on Tuesday, with showers expected to continue through October 13.Bihar may also receive isolated to scattered rainfall on Tuesday. The IMD has forecast another spell of rainfall over the state during October 15-18, with thunderstorms, lightning and gusty winds reaching 30-40 kmph, with gusts up to 50 kmph, likely at isolated places during October 16-18.Odisha is likely to receive isolated to scattered rainfall during October 12-18.The Andaman and Nicobar Islands are also expected to experience isolated to scattered rainfall during the same period.Northeast India weather forecastSeveral parts of the Northeast are likely to receive rainfall over the coming days.Nagaland, Manipur, Mizoram and Tripura are likely to experience isolated to scattered rainfall from October 12 to 18. Assam and Meghalaya may receive showers during October 13-18, while Arunachal Pradesh is likely to see rainfall during October 15-18.The forecast indicates continued rainfall activity across the region through the middle and latter parts of the week.South India weather tomorrowSeveral parts of south India are likely to experience rainfall, thunderstorms and gusty winds on Tuesday.Coastal Andhra Pradesh and Yanam, Rayalaseema, Coastal Karnataka and Tamil Nadu, Puducherry and Karaikal are likely to receive isolated to scattered rainfall during October 12-18.Kerala and Mahe may also receive isolated to scattered rainfall during October 12-14, while Lakshadweep is likely to experience showers during October 12-15.The IMD has forecast thunderstorms, lightning and gusty winds reaching 40-50 kmph, with gusts up to 60 kmph, over Tamil Nadu, Puducherry and Karaikal during October 12-15. Kerala and Mahe may experience similar conditions during October 14-15.Coastal Andhra Pradesh and Yanam, along with Rayalaseema, are likely to experience gusty winds reaching 30-40 kmph, with gusts up to 50 kmph, during October 12-15. Strong surface winds are also likely over these regions during the same period.Thunderstorms and lightning are likely over Kerala and Mahe on October 12-13.IMD's latest forecast for the next few daysRainfall activity is expected to continue across several parts of India through October 18, with northwest, central, eastern and southern regions likely to experience varying spells of showers.In northwest India, rainfall is forecast over parts of Jammu and Kashmir, Ladakh, Himachal Pradesh, Uttarakhand, Punjab, Haryana, Chandigarh, Delhi and Uttar Pradesh. Punjab may experience fairly widespread to widespread rainfall on October 15.In south India, Kerala and Mahe are likely to receive fairly widespread to widespread rainfall during October 15-18. Lakshadweep and South Interior Karnataka may also experience fairly widespread to widespread rainfall during October 16-18.Heavy rainfall is likely at isolated places over Kerala and Mahe, as well as Tamil Nadu, Puducherry and Karaikal, during October 16-18.Meanwhile, rainfall is expected to continue across Chhattisgarh, Odisha, the Andaman and Nicobar Islands and parts of the Northeast during the coming days.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Delhi | Silver Rate in Delhi | Bank Holidays in Delhi | Public Holidays in Delhi | Delhi AQI | Weather in Delhi | Petrol Price in Delhi | Diesel Price in Delhi | CNG Price in Delhi | LPG Price in DelhiStay updated with the latest Delhi news. articles.title: 'Your people don’t even let us go near the aircraft':  As IAF trains with F-35 fighters, US guards secrets
articles.summary: The US Air Force has been protective of the F-35 at the second edition of Exercise Tarang Shakti.
articles.body: The US Air Force has been protective of the F-35 at the second edition of Exercise Tarang Shakti. This was the first time that the advanced fifth-generation fighter has flown in India airspace in an operational manner. The F-35 has made appearances at the Aero India, a biennial aerospace and defence exhibition held at Yelahanka in Bengaluru. Air Chief Marshal AP Singh, while seated next to General Kevin Schneider, Commander of the US Pacific Air Forces, during a press conference in Jodhpur stated “Your people don’t even let us go near the aircraft, and you talk about selling it to us.” The IAF Chief also said, in response to another question that “The US did not show us the cockpit, but allowed us to fly in close formation.”General Schneider did clarify that the decision was not his to make. Programme-level security classification guides, he said, determine what can be shared, when it is shared and how it is protected.The importance of fifth-generation fightersFifth generation aircraft are built to reduce their radar cross-section through advanced composite airframes, careful shaping, internal weapons bays and radar-absorbent materials, which helps them survive in contested airspace. They also fuse data from the AESA radar, distributed aperture system, electronic warfare suite and infrared search-and-track sensors into a single real-time picture for the pilot. Designed to work in a network, they continuously receive information from airborne early warning aircraft, satellites, ground sensors and other fighters, giving pilots situational awareness that has changed how air combat is fought, giving the air crew an edge.India's own route to such a jet is the Advanced Medium Combat Aircraft. Earlier this month, the Chief called for the programme to be accelerated, warning that further delays could force the service to look at alternative fifth-generation fighters. He said Russia had offered the Su-57, but no decision had been taken on it. He also voiced concern over Pakistan's reported efforts to acquire fifth-generation fighters with Chinese assistance, while maintaining that India has the capability to counter such threats through an integrated military system. At the same time the air force chief has described unmanned aerial systems as evolutionary rather than revolutionary for the IAF, which has operated them for decades. The force is expanding their number and types, he said, and loitering munitions have helped disrupt enemy air-defence assets.The air force has also flagged delays in Tejas Mk-1A deliveries, which are weighing on the IAF's declining fighter strength. The force is counting on the Tejas Mk-1A, the underdevelopment Tejas Mk-2 and additional 114 Rafale aircraft to bridge its capability gaps. On Sunday, the Chief flew a Tejas fighter from the Jodhpur airbase, his last flight before he retires on October 31. The IAF currently operates initial and final operational clearance configurations as it awaits the Tejas Mk-1A.

articles.title: A Michigan couple bought land at a 2015 tax sale and claimed a 50-foot strip lost through a 1965 deed error; after two surveys put it with their neighbour, an appeals court ruled against them
articles.summary: A couple in Michigan, United States, has lost a legal battle over a 50-foot-wide strip of land that they claimed belonged to their property because of an
articles.body: A couple in Michigan, United States, has lost a legal battle over a 50-foot-wide strip of land that they claimed belonged to their property because of an error in a deed dating back to 1965. Max W. Firman III and Dawn M. Kasner, who purchased their land at a tax sale in 2015, argued that the disputed strip had been used by previous owners of their property for decades. However, the Michigan Court of Appeals ruled against them on Friday, finding that they had not provided enough evidence to establish ownership.According to court documents, the dispute involved neighbouring properties in Rose Township, Ogemaw County. Firman and Kasner bought their parcel in 2015, while their neighbour, Antonio Santos, purchased the surrounding property in 2021. The disagreement began when Santos challenged the couple's claim over the strip of land, which also contained a structure.The couple believed that a mistake made in a 1965 tax sale deed had changed the description of their property's boundary. They relied on an earlier deed from 1955, which referred to a boundary measurement of 400 feet. However, the 1965 deed used 450 feet, and that description continued to appear in subsequent property records.The difference of 50 feet became the centre of the dispute. Although the couple claimed that the land and the structure on it had been used by previous owners of their property, two surveys commissioned by Santos placed the disputed area within his property. The disagreement eventually reached the courts, where the couple sought legal recognition of their ownership.How a 1965 deed became the centre of the disputeThe couple argued that the change in the property description in 1965 was an error that had remained uncorrected for decades. They maintained that the disputed strip should have been included with the land they purchased in 2015.They also claimed that previous owners had built, maintained and used the structure located on the disputed land. According to their case, they continued using the area after purchasing the property and believed that taxes had been paid on it by them and earlier owners.Santos disputed these claims. After buying the surrounding property in 2021, he commissioned two surveys, both of which showed that the 50-foot strip belonged to his property.He also submitted a photograph of the structure taken before the 2015 tax sale. A sign on the building read "NOT IN TAX SALE". Santos said his immediate predecessor had placed the sign there because photographs used in the tax sale listing had created the impression that the disputed area was included in the property being sold.Disagreement escalated after locks were changedThe dispute became more serious after Santos purchased his property. Both sides accused each other of entering the disputed area without permission.In 2023, the local sheriff was contacted after Santos allegedly changed the locks on the structure and demolished some interior walls. The sheriff told the couple that the ownership dispute would have to be settled in court.Firman and Kasner filed a lawsuit in February 2024, seeking to establish ownership of the disputed land and raising a trespass claim. Santos responded with counterclaims, including trespass and nuisance.The trial court subsequently ruled in Santos's favour, finding that the couple's original claim was barred by Michigan's 15-year limitation period. The couple then amended their complaint, arguing that they and previous owners had acquired ownership through adverse possession or acquiescence.What evidence did the couple present?To support their case, the couple submitted a 1982 deed and a 2013 affidavit concerning earlier owners of their property.The 1982 deed referred to land possessed by the previous owners for more than 15 years "in this vicinity". The couple argued that this showed the earlier owners had already acquired rights over the disputed area.The 2013 affidavit also referred to an adverse possession claim by a previous owner, Vianne Samuels, concerning property interests not clearly established in the recorded ownership documents.Adverse possession is a legal principle under which someone may acquire ownership of land through possession that meets specific legal requirements over a prescribed period. In Michigan, the relevant period is 15 years.However, the appeals court found that neither document identified the disputed 50-foot strip. Both also continued to use the same property description found in the 1965 deed.The couple relied on tax records and the existence of the structure as further evidence. But the court found that these records did not establish who had built or used the structure, when it was built, or whether the disputed land had been openly and continuously possessed for the required period.Michigan appeals court ruled against the coupleThe appeals court also considered the couple's argument of acquiescence, under which neighbouring owners may establish a property boundary by treating it as the accepted boundary for 15 years.The judges found insufficient evidence that previous owners of the neighbouring properties had accepted the boundary claimed by the couple. The sign stating "NOT IN TAX SALE" also indicated that Santos's immediate predecessor had not accepted their claimed boundary.In its October 9 ruling, the Michigan Court of Appeals upheld the trial court's decision dismissing the couple's amended complaint.However, the case has not ended entirely. The appeals court sent it back to the trial court for further proceedings concerning Santos's outstanding counterclaims, which were not decided in the appeal.You use AI every day. articles.title: A bus route that served two worlds disappears from BEST's travel map
articles.summary: MUMBAI: The familiar red BEST bus once left Borivli station (East) before dawn, carrying vegetable and fruit vendors to Vashi's APMC market.
articles.body: MUMBAI: The familiar red BEST bus once left Borivli station (East) before dawn, carrying vegetable and fruit vendors to Vashi's APMC market. Later, office-goers, IT professionals and private-sector employees used it to travel from Navi Mumbai towards Powai, SEEPZ, Andheri and Goregaon. After years of curtailment, BEST discontinued Route A471, formerly 524L, this month.Bus enthusiast and commuter Shubham Padave, campaigning for its revival for four years, has proposed four to five morning and evening peak-hour trips via the Eastern Express Highway, using newly inducted blade-battery electric buses with greater range. The route's decline began in July 2021, when most trips were curtailed to Ghatkopar depot. By September, buses no longer reached Vashi. In September 2024, the Borivli-Ghatkopar service became air-conditioned and was renamed A471.Passenger frequency fell until only one trip remained. BEST officials cited "low passenger response" for the cancellation. A senior official said curtailed or cancelled routes could be reviewed once more buses became available.Regular commuters Harish Kulkarni and Meeta Salvi also urged BEST to restart the route with a few peak-hour trips, expanding the service when buses become available. Priti Mhatre, a Goregaon commuter, said its loss meant losing a direct, affordable connection that saved time and multiple transfers.BEST said commuters could use parallel routes 489 Ltd and A-470, or A-458 and A-460 from Gandhi Nagar.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Mumbai | Silver Rate in Mumbai | Bank Holidays in Mumbai | Public Holidays in Mumbai | Mumbai AQI | Weather in Mumbai | Petrol Price in Mumbai | Diesel Price in Mumbai | CNG Price in Mumbai | LPG Price in MumbaiStay updated with the latest Mumbai news.
